question: What made you want to study animation?
lookingFor: A genuine, specific origin for the interest rather than a vague love of cartoons.

bullets: Name a specific moment, film, or piece of work that sparked it
Explain what about animation specifically pulled you in, not just storytelling in general
Connect it to something you've actually made or attempted since
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I got properly hooked when I first watched the making-of footage for a Studio Ghibli film and saw how much motion could carry emotion without a single word of dialogue. That sent me down a rabbit hole of learning how animators time a single glance to make a character feel nervous. I started messing around with a cheap tablet and looping a two-second walk cycle for a week, and I realised I loved the obsessive, patient side of it just as much as the storytelling.

commonMistakes: Saying 'I've always loved cartoons' with nothing more specific
Talking only about liking stories, with nothing about the craft of animating
Not backing it up with anything they've actually made or tried
followUps: What was the first thing you ever tried to animate yourself?

question: Why do you want to study animation here specifically, rather than another course or a self-taught route?
lookingFor: Evidence of real research into the course structure and honest reasoning for choosing formal study over self-teaching.

bullets: Reference a specific strength of the course, such as its pipeline modules, facilities, or a named tutor's work
Explain what structured study gives you that YouTube tutorials and forums don't
Show awareness of what makes this course distinct from similar ones
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I taught myself the basics on free software for two years, but I kept hitting a ceiling because I had no one to tell me why a shot wasn't reading, only whether I liked it or not. Your course's structure, where you rotate through 2D, stop-motion, and CG in the first year before specialising, is exactly what I need, because I genuinely don't know yet which discipline suits me best. I also looked at the degree show reels from the last two years and the character work stood out as stronger and more consistent than anywhere else I applied.

commonMistakes: Generic praise about facilities that would fit any animation school
No real answer for why formal study over self-teaching
Confusing this course's pathway with a different institution's
followUps: What would you do in your first year if you could design your own project?

question: Tell us about the first time you remember being genuinely fascinated by how an animation was made, not just what it showed.
lookingFor: A specific, personal memory that shows curiosity about craft rather than just consumption of content.

bullets: Pick one concrete memory, not a general lifelong interest
Describe what specifically caught your attention about the technique
Show how that curiosity changed what you did afterward
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I was maybe twelve and rewatching a scene where a character's cape moved completely differently depending on how fast they were running, and I remember pausing and rewinding it about ten times trying to understand why it looked so convincing. I later found out that was secondary motion, one of the animation principles, and once I had the name for it I started noticing it everywhere, in flags, hair, even the way people's sleeves move when they wave. That's when I started actually looking things up instead of just watching.

commonMistakes: Giving a generic answer about loving Disney films as a kid
Focusing entirely on plot or characters rather than the animation itself
No follow-through describing what they did after that moment
followUps: Do you still notice that kind of detail when you watch animation now?

question: Talk us through a piece in your portfolio you're proudest of, and one you'd do differently now.
lookingFor: Ability to discuss your own work critically and specifically, showing growth and self-awareness rather than just pride.

bullets: Describe the piece concretely: what it was, what challenge it solved
Explain specifically why you're proud of it, tied to a craft decision
Name a genuine weakness or thing you'd change, showing you can self-critique
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'm proudest of a short walk cycle I did of an old man carrying heavy shopping bags, because I spent real time studying how weight shifts the whole body, not just the arms, and I think the shuffle in his step actually reads as tired. If I did it again I'd loosen up the arcs, because looking back the path of his hands is a bit too straight and mechanical in places. That piece taught me I was thinking about timing more than spacing, and I've been trying to fix that balance since.

commonMistakes: Only describing the piece with no critical reflection
Being falsely modest and unable to name a genuine strength
Vague answers like 'I'd make it better' with no specific fix named
followUps: How did you get feedback on that piece, and what did you do with it?

question: Can you name a few of the classic principles of animation and explain one in detail?
lookingFor: Genuine familiarity with the Disney twelve principles and the ability to explain one with a concrete example.

bullets: Name at least two or three principles correctly
Pick one and explain what it actually does for the audience
Give a concrete visual example, not just the definition
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: There are twelve classic ones from the old Disney animators, things like squash and stretch, anticipation, follow-through, and timing. I find anticipation the most interesting, it's the small preparatory movement before the main action, like a character winding up before they throw a punch. Without it the action reads as sudden and confusing, but even a few frames of a shoulder pulling back tells the audience's eye where to look and makes the punch land with much more weight.

commonMistakes: Naming the principles but unable to explain any in real depth
Confusing principles with unrelated animation terms like keyframing
Giving a textbook definition with no visual example
followUps: Can you think of a principle that's harder to apply in 3D than in 2D, or vice versa?

question: What is squash and stretch, and why does it matter?
lookingFor: A clear, correct explanation of the principle plus why it adds believability rather than just being decoration.

bullets: Explain the deformation itself: an object squashing on impact and stretching in motion
Mention that volume should generally stay consistent through the deformation
Explain why it matters: it sells weight, flexibility, and speed
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Squash and stretch is when an object deforms as it moves, so a bouncing ball flattens when it hits the ground and stretches out when it's falling fast. The important part is that its overall volume should stay roughly the same, it's not shrinking or growing, just changing shape. Without it, motion feels stiff and lifeless, because in real life almost nothing is perfectly rigid, and even a subtle squash on a character's cheek when they land from a jump makes the impact feel real.

commonMistakes: Describing it only as making things 'bouncy' with no mention of volume
Confusing it with a different principle like exaggeration
Unable to explain why it matters beyond 'it looks nice'
followUps: Can you think of a case where too much squash and stretch would look wrong?

question: Do you prefer 2D or 3D animation, and why?
lookingFor: A reasoned preference grounded in understanding the actual differences in workflow, not just which looks nicer.

bullets: State a genuine preference or explain why you're undecided
Point to a real workflow or expressive difference between the two, not just visual style
Show openness to the discipline you prefer less
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I lean toward 2D, mostly because I love that every frame is a fresh drawing decision, which lets you push a pose or an expression further than a rig usually allows. But I've done a bit of 3D too and I respect how much of the craft moves into the rigging and the graph editor, it's a different kind of problem-solving rather than an easier one. I want this course precisely because it doesn't let me specialise immediately, since I suspect I'd actually enjoy 3D character animation more than I currently think.

commonMistakes: Dismissing the other discipline as inferior or 'not real animation'
Basing the answer purely on which looks prettier with no craft reasoning
Not actually knowing any real differences between the two workflows
followUps: What do you think is the hardest transferable skill between 2D and 3D animation?

question: Which animation studio or director's work do you admire most, and why?
lookingFor: A specific, well-argued taste that goes beyond naming a popular studio, showing real engagement with technique or storytelling.

bullets: Name a specific studio, director, or animator, not just a genre or franchise
Explain what specifically about their work you admire, in craft terms
Show you've seen more than one piece of their output
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I keep coming back to Studio Laika, particularly Kubo and the Two Strings, because stop-motion at that scale is such a stubborn, patient craft, every tiny facial expression is a physically printed piece swapped by hand. What gets me is how they use that limitation to their advantage, the slight imperfection in the puppets' movement gives everything a tactile weight that CG often struggles to fake. I've watched the behind-the-scenes documentaries for most of their films because I find the problem-solving as compelling as the finished result.

commonMistakes: Naming a huge franchise with no specific craft reasoning
Only referencing one film with no sense of a broader body of work
Talking about plot or characters with nothing about animation technique
followUps: Is there anything about their work you'd want to do differently yourself?

question: Is there an individual animator, past or present, whose work has particularly influenced you?
lookingFor: Depth of research into the field beyond famous studios, and an ability to articulate what specifically was learned from that person.

bullets: Name a specific animator, not just a studio or franchise
Explain what technique, philosophy, or approach you learned from studying their work
Connect it to something in your own practice
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Richard Williams' book on the animator's survival kit was honestly what taught me to actually think about spacing rather than just drawing pretty poses. His breakdown of how to chart out timing before touching the final drawings changed how I plan my own shots, I now rough out a timing chart on paper before I animate anything. What I admire most is that he treated animation as a rigorous, almost mathematical craft underneath the artistry, and that combination is exactly what drew me to want formal training.

commonMistakes: Naming only a studio or a film rather than an individual
Vague admiration with no specific technique or lesson named
No connection back to their own developing practice
followUps: Have you read any other books or resources on animation craft?

question: What do you understand about how stop-motion animation is made, and what makes it different to work with?
lookingFor: Basic technical understanding of the stop-motion process and awareness of what makes it distinct in constraints and appeal.

bullets: Describe the basic process: physical models moved incrementally and shot frame by frame
Mention a real constraint, such as needing consistent lighting, armatures, or replacement parts
Explain what it offers that digital animation doesn't
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Stop-motion works by physically posing a model, usually built on a metal armature so it holds a pose, taking a single photograph, then nudging it very slightly and shooting the next frame. It's unforgiving because you can't undo a bad frame the way you can in digital software, and lighting has to stay locked down for weeks so continuity doesn't flicker. What draws me to it is that every tiny imperfection in the movement is real and physical, there's a texture to it that even very good CGI struggles to fake.

commonMistakes: Confusing stop-motion with claymation as if the terms are identical
No mention of the practical constraints like lighting or continuity
Describing it as an outdated technique with nothing about its ongoing appeal
followUps: Have you ever tried making anything in stop-motion yourself?

question: What role does a storyboard play in making an animated piece, and what makes a good one?
lookingFor: Understanding that storyboarding is a planning and communication tool, not just rough drawing, with a sense of what makes one effective.

bullets: Explain storyboarding as planning shot composition, staging, and story flow before expensive production begins
Mention it as a communication tool for a team, not just personal notes
Name a quality of a good board, such as clear staging or readable poses even in rough form
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A storyboard maps out every shot before anyone commits time to actual animation, so you catch pacing problems or confusing staging cheaply, on paper, rather than after weeks of work. It also has to communicate clearly to other people, a director or the rest of a team, so even rough thumbnails need readable poses and a clear sense of where the eye should go in each frame. A good board tells the whole story even in silhouette, you should be able to follow what's happening without any dialogue or colour.

commonMistakes: Describing it as just 'drawing the scenes' with no mention of planning function
Missing that it's a communication tool for a wider team
No sense of what separates a clear board from a messy one
followUps: Have you ever had to redo a storyboard after realising the pacing didn't work?

question: What does animating 'on twos' mean, and why would an animator choose it over animating on every single frame?
lookingFor: Correct technical understanding of a basic term plus reasoning about the creative and practical trade-off involved.

bullets: Explain that animating on twos means holding each drawing for two frames instead of one
Note the practical benefit: roughly half the drawings for the same length of footage
Mention the creative trade-off: it can give a slightly punchier, more stylised feel versus the smoothness of ones
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Animating on twos means each drawing is held for two frames instead of one, so at twenty-four frames per second you're only actually drawing twelve unique images per second of footage. It's partly practical, since hand-drawn animation is so time-consuming that halving the drawing count matters a lot, but it's also a stylistic choice, a lot of classic animation actually looks punchier on twos rather than smoother. Ones are usually saved for fast action or especially important moments where you want maximum fluidity.

commonMistakes: Confusing 'on twos' with a frame rate like 24fps itself
Only mentioning the time-saving reason with no creative reasoning
Getting the drawing count backwards
followUps: When might an animator deliberately switch to ones mid-shot?

question: What is a rig in 3D animation, and why does a good one matter to an animator?
lookingFor: Basic correct understanding of rigging as the control skeleton for a model, and awareness of how it affects the animator's work directly.

bullets: Explain a rig as the underlying skeleton and control system that lets a static model be posed and moved
Distinguish the rigger's job from the animator's job
Explain why rig quality directly affects what an animator can achieve
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A rig is essentially the skeleton and set of controls built inside a 3D model that let an animator actually pose and move it, rather than pushing raw geometry around by hand. It's usually built by a rigger, a separate role from the animator, though on smaller projects one person does both. A badly built rig can genuinely limit what you're able to animate, if the shoulder doesn't deform properly when the arm lifts, no amount of animating skill fixes that, so a good rig is really the foundation everything else depends on.

commonMistakes: Confusing rigging with modelling or texturing
Treating rigging and animating as interchangeable jobs
No sense of why rig quality actually constrains the animator
followUps: Have you used any rigged characters yourself, even pre-built ones?

question: How would you go about designing a character to visually communicate their personality before they even move or speak?
lookingFor: Understanding of silhouette, shape language, and visual storytelling as tools for character design, not just drawing skill.

bullets: Mention shape language, how rounded, angular, or square forms suggest different personality traits
Emphasise silhouette readability as a test of clear design
Give a concrete example connecting a design choice to a personality trait
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think in terms of shape language first, rounded forms tend to read as friendly or soft, while sharp angular shapes read as threatening or rigid, so I try to build a character's silhouette around whichever feeling fits them. I always test it in pure black silhouette, because if you can't tell what a character is doing or roughly who they are from the outline alone, the design isn't doing its job yet. For a nervous, timid character I'd lean into narrower shoulders and a slightly hunched, smaller silhouette, so the audience reads their personality before they've said a word.

commonMistakes: Focusing only on clothing or colour with no mention of shape or silhouette
Describing design purely in terms of drawing skill rather than communication
No concrete example connecting a design choice to a trait
followUps: Can you think of a well-known character whose silhouette alone tells you who they are?

question: What animation or drawing software have you used, and what have you learned from working in it?
lookingFor: Honest account of real hands-on experience, showing they've actually worked with tools rather than just knowing names.

bullets: Name specific software actually used, not just software they've heard of
Describe a concrete thing they made or struggled with in it
Show awareness that software is a tool, not the point of the craft
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I've mostly worked in a free program called Blender for a bit of 3D, and I use a tablet with a program similar to Photoshop for frame-by-frame 2D work. Blender was frustrating at first because the interface has a steep learning curve, but working through a basic bouncing ball tutorial actually taught me more about timing than any of my 2D attempts had, because you can see the graph editor curves directly. I know the software itself will change and that studios often use different packages, so I try to focus on understanding the underlying principle rather than memorising menus.

commonMistakes: Listing software names with no evidence of actually using them
Treating software fluency as the main qualification rather than fundamentals
No specific project or struggle mentioned
followUps: What was the hardest thing to learn in that software?

question: Have you watched any animation outside the mainstream studio films that shaped how you think about the craft?
lookingFor: Genuine curiosity and exposure beyond the obvious big-studio references, showing initiative in seeking out the field.

bullets: Name something specific and less obvious, such as an independent short, a foreign studio, or an experimental piece
Explain what specifically it showed them that mainstream work hadn't
Show this was self-directed curiosity, not an assigned viewing
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I went through a phase of watching short films from festivals like Annecy on YouTube, and one that stuck with me was a hand-painted short that used almost no dialogue and completely broke the twelve-frame consistency rule, the texture changed shot to shot on purpose. It showed me that a lot of what I'd assumed were fixed rules of animation are really just conventions of big studio pipelines, and that experimental work can use imperfection expressively. It made me want to try something rougher and more painterly myself instead of always chasing polish.

commonMistakes: Only naming mainstream feature films everyone has seen
No explanation of what was actually learned from it
Vague claims of watching 'a lot of animation' with no specifics
followUps: Did it change anything about how you approach your own work?

question: Some people say technically flawless animation with a weak story fails, but a strong story can survive rough animation. Do you agree?
lookingFor: Nuanced judgement that weighs both craft and story rather than picking an extreme, with reasoning and examples.

bullets: Avoid a simplistic either/or answer, acknowledge both matter differently at different scales
Give a concrete example supporting the reasoning
Land on a considered position rather than refusing to commit
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I mostly agree that story carries further than polish, a lot of beloved student films and early web animations have rough linework but people remember them because a character's want or fear came through clearly. But I don't think it's absolute, some purely technical work, like an experimental short exploring motion itself, isn't really trying to tell a story in the first place, so judging it on story would miss the point. My honest view is that story is what makes an audience care, but craft is what makes them believe it, and you need at least a workable amount of both.

commonMistakes: Picking one side absolutely with no nuance
No concrete example to support the reasoning
Refusing to actually take a position
followUps: Can you think of a specific film where you felt this trade-off went wrong?

question: Tell us about a recent animated film you have mixed feelings about. What worked and what didn't, in your view?
lookingFor: Ability to give a balanced, specific critique grounded in craft observation rather than a simple review of liking or disliking it.

bullets: Name a specific film, not a vague category
Point to a specific craft element that worked, with a reason
Point to a specific weakness, again grounded in craft rather than just taste
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I have mixed feelings about a recent CG feature where the character animation was genuinely excellent, the facial performance in the quiet dialogue scenes felt more honest than a lot of live action I've seen. But I thought the environment lighting was overly flat in the middle act, it made otherwise strong staging feel a bit lifeless, like the camera was floating through a video game rather than a lived-in world. I think it's a good example of how uneven craft across departments can undercut work that individually is very strong.

commonMistakes: Vague praise or criticism with no specific craft detail
Reviewing the plot rather than the animation itself
Refusing to name any real weakness out of fear of seeming negative
followUps: If you'd directed that section, what would you have changed?

question: Animation courses involve a lot of group critique of your work. How do you handle being told a piece you're attached to isn't working?
lookingFor: Genuine openness to critique with a real example, showing they can separate their ego from their work.

bullets: Give a concrete example of receiving tough feedback, not a hypothetical
Show they actually listened and made a change, rather than just tolerating the comment
Reflect on what the experience taught them about their own work
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I once brought a short piece to a critique group that I'd spent weeks on, convinced the timing was fine, and someone pointed out that the main action read as accidental because there was no anticipation before it. My first reaction was defensive, but I sat with it overnight and realised they were right, I'd gotten so close to the piece I couldn't see it fresh anymore. I redid just that beat with a few extra frames of wind-up, and it genuinely fixed the read, so now I try to actively invite that kind of blunt feedback early rather than waiting until I'm too attached to change anything.

commonMistakes: Claiming they always take feedback well with no real example
Describing a story where they simply ignored the feedback and were vindicated
No reflection on what they actually learned
followUps: Has feedback ever changed your mind about a whole approach, not just a detail?

subtopic: Choosing animation over live action or fine art
question: You could tell stories through live-action film or work purely in illustration. Why animation specifically?
lookingFor: A clear articulation of what animation uniquely offers as a medium, showing deliberate choice rather than defaulting into it.

bullets: Name something animation can do that live action or static illustration can't
Ground it in a personal reason, not just an abstract claim
Show respect for the other mediums rather than dismissing them
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: What animation gives me that live action doesn't is total control, every single frame is a deliberate choice, there's no lighting accident or actor's off-day to work around, which suits how meticulous I am. And compared to illustration, it adds time, a single drawing can only imply movement, but animation lets me actually build the anticipation and follow-through that makes an emotion land. I don't think either of the other mediums is lesser, I just think animation is the one where my particular patience and love of small physical detail actually pays off.

commonMistakes: Dismissing live action or illustration as inferior rather than just different
Giving an answer that could apply equally to any visual medium
No personal reasoning connecting the choice to themselves
followUps: Is there anything live action does better than animation, in your view?

question: What is the uncanny valley, and why do you think it matters for animators working on realistic human characters?
lookingFor: Correct understanding of the concept plus thoughtful reasoning about its practical implications for character design choices.

bullets: Explain the concept: as characters approach photorealism, near-perfect but imperfect ones can feel unsettling rather than more likeable
Note it's not linear, very stylised characters can be highly likeable despite being far from realistic
Discuss a practical implication for design or animation choices
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The uncanny valley describes how, as a character's design gets closer to photorealistic human, audience comfort with it doesn't rise smoothly, it actually dips sharply right before reaching true realism, because small imperfections in something almost-human read as unsettling rather than charming. It's part of why a lot of successful CG characters are deliberately stylised rather than fully photoreal, a slightly exaggerated proportion or simplified eye can be more likeable than an almost-perfect human face. For animators it matters practically because it means chasing more realism isn't automatically the safer choice, sometimes pulling back on realism is what actually makes a character land emotionally.

commonMistakes: Vaguely describing it as 'creepy robots' with no real explanation of the mechanism
Missing that the effect is non-linear, not simply 'more realistic is worse'
No practical implication drawn for actual design choices
followUps: Can you think of a character you've seen that you felt fell into the uncanny valley?

question: Animated characters are often built from simplified, exaggerated visual traits. Where do you think the line is between expressive character design and harmful stereotyping?
lookingFor: Thoughtful ethical reasoning showing awareness of the tension between exaggeration as a craft tool and its potential for harm, not a simplistic verdict.

bullets: Acknowledge that exaggeration is a genuine, necessary tool of the medium, not inherently wrong
Explain what tips exaggeration into harm, such as when traits map onto real marginalised groups in demeaning ways
Show how they'd handle it practically in their own design choices
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Exaggeration is honestly core to how animation communicates, a character's whole appeal often comes from pushing a feature further than realism would allow, so I don't think simplification itself is the problem. Where it becomes stereotyping is when those exaggerated traits consistently map onto a real ethnicity, body type, or identity in a way that's demeaning or reduces a whole group to a punchline, especially when it's the only representation that group gets in a story. In my own work I try to ask whether I'd be comfortable if the trait I'm exaggerating were the only thing that character was known for, and if the answer's no, I go back and design something more specific to that individual character rather than a type.

commonMistakes: Claiming exaggeration is always fine because 'it's just cartoons'
Refusing to engage and saying it's entirely subjective with no reasoning
No practical answer for how they'd handle it in their own design work
followUps: Can you think of an example where a studio got this balance wrong, in your view?

question: A few seconds of finished animation can take days of repetitive, painstaking work. How do you know you'll cope with that reality?
lookingFor: Realistic understanding of the labour involved and evidence from their own experience that they can sustain patient, repetitive work.

bullets: Show realistic awareness of how slow and repetitive real animation work is
Give a concrete personal example of sustaining a long, tedious task
Explain what keeps them motivated through the tedious stretches
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I already got a taste of this doing a ten-second walk cycle that took me almost two weeks of evenings, redrawing the same few frames dozens of times to fix a wobble in the arc of the hand. It was genuinely tedious in places, but I noticed that breaking it into small, specific problems, like just fixing one arc at a time, kept it from feeling overwhelming. What keeps me motivated is seeing the playblast improve even slightly each pass, that small feedback loop is honestly what I enjoy about the craft, not just the finished product.

commonMistakes: Claiming they'll simply 'push through' with no real strategy or evidence
Underestimating how slow real animation work actually is
No concrete personal example of having sustained tedious work before
followUps: What do you do when you hit a point where a shot just isn't working, no matter how many times you redo it?

question: What's the difference between timing and spacing in animation, and why do animators talk about them as separate things?
lookingFor: Clear technical understanding that timing controls speed via frame count while spacing controls the distribution of drawings, and why both are needed.

bullets: Define timing as how many frames an action takes, controlling speed
Define spacing as how the individual drawings are distributed within that time, controlling acceleration and feel
Explain why both matter together, not interchangeably
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Timing is basically how many frames an action takes overall, so a punch that takes six frames reads as much faster than one that takes twenty. Spacing is different, it's about how those drawings are distributed within that time, whether they're bunched close together or spread evenly apart, and that's what actually controls whether something feels like it's accelerating or moving at a constant speed. You need both, because two actions can have identical timing but completely different spacing, one might ease in gently while the other snaps sharply, and that difference is what makes movement feel alive rather than mechanical.

commonMistakes: Treating timing and spacing as the same thing
Defining one correctly but confusing the other
No explanation of why the distinction actually matters to the final feel
followUps: How would you show a character hesitating using spacing alone?

question: Animation covers many different roles, from character animation to background art to rigging. Do you have a sense of which direction interests you, and why?
lookingFor: Realistic awareness of the range of specialist roles in the field and a grounded, if tentative, sense of personal direction.

bullets: Show awareness that animation involves many distinct specialist roles, not just 'being an animator'
Name a direction of interest with a concrete reason tied to their own strengths or experience
Show openness to changing direction once they've tried more disciplines
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Right now I'm most drawn to character animation, specifically performance and acting through movement, because the projects I've enjoyed most have all been about getting a tiny gesture to convey a feeling. But I know background and layout art, rigging, and technical direction are all their own serious specialisms, and I've only really tried character work so far, so I'm genuinely open to discovering I actually prefer something else once I've had a proper go at the others. That's part of why I want a course that rotates through disciplines before making me choose.

commonMistakes: Answering as if 'animator' is a single undifferentiated job
Naming a direction with no personal reasoning behind it
Sounding completely fixed and unwilling to explore other roles
followUps: What's a role in the pipeline you know least about, and would want to learn?
